coverageNote: Enumerated from disk: 8 units (the domain directory itself plus 7 sub-domain directories, each containing an *-index.md), 48 .md files total — exactly matching the expected 8 units / 48 files. All 48 files were read. Structural claims were verified programmatically against disk: the domain index's claim of '10 leaves [DEEP], 13 [PARTIAL], 9 [SURFACE]' across 32 leaf features tallies exactly (10/13/9, 32 leaves, 7 sub-domains). A repo-wide relative-link resolution check was run across all 48 files; 1 of ~180 links is broken (finding #006). A repo-wide scan for bare `[PENDING]` markers (no owner, no deferral target) was run; 22 occurrences were classified, of which 6 are genuinely untracked and are reported (findings #004, #011, #012, #013) and the rest resolve to a properly-owned Open Question row. This tree is unusually mature: the great majority of open decisions carry an explicit owner and deferral target, contradictions surfaced during deepening are explicitly reconciled in the CX files (05.05 CX-01 Q5 and 05.07 CX Q5 are both correctly updated to cite their resolving decisions), and normative thresholds are stated as numbers rather than adjectives throughout. Findings are correspondingly sparse and concentrated in 05.03/05.04.

scoring.naRationale: Dimensions 1 (Problem Clarity), 2 (Persona Specificity) and 4 (Constraint Explicitness) are N/A across every unit: they are owned by meta/problem-statement.md, meta/personas.md and meta/constraints.md respectively, which are outside this domain's scope. The domain index explicitly states personas are 'Never redefined here — referenced only' (D-19). Dimension 6 (Competitive Positioning) is applicable ONLY to the domain unit, whose Overview names three competitors and a specific capability gap; it is N/A for the seven sub-domain units, which are not positioning documents. Dimensions 3, 5, 7 and 8 apply to all 8 units.

findings.claim: Two unmarked normative decisions give opposite answers to the same race: whether a revision request submitted in the 120 seconds AFTER the auto-accept deadline cancels auto-accept or loses to it. 05.03.03 D-10 makes the deadline a hard boundary; 05.04.01 D-04 adds a 120-second grace past it. Neither cites the other as superseded, and each file claims to own the rule.
findings.evidence: 05.03-engagement-lifecycle/05.03.03-revisions-limits-change-orders.md:222 — "| D-10 | **A revision request submitted before the auto-accept expiry wins the race** against auto-accept | Auto-accept punishes inaction; a buyer who acted was not inactive. Same reasoning CX-01 applied to requirements supply. Mechanism (single authoritative clock, submission not receipt) is `/create-prd-architecture`'s. |"  ·  05.03.03:126 — "| **Revision request lands as auto-accept fires** | **The request wins if its submission timestamp precedes the window's expiry.**"  ·  CONTRADICTED BY 05.04-delivery-qc-acceptance/05.04.01-delivery-acceptance-auto-accept.md:213 — "| D-04 | **Revision beats auto-accept in a tie**, via an invisible **120-second grace** after the deadline."  ·  05.04.01:114 — "A **120-second grace** follows the deadline. Any revision request received at or before deadline+120s wins and cancels auto-accept; anything after loses and is routed to recall (05.03.06, per 05.03.03 D-05)."  ·  Ownership is also contested: 05.03.03:196 Cross-Cut Notes says "the simultaneous-fire precedence rule is D-10 here and the mechanism is theirs (their Q-03)", while 05.04.01 Q-03 reads "✅ **RESOLVED** — precedence when a revision request and auto-accept fire simultaneously. See D-04".
findings.forcedInvention: The implementer must invent whether the auto-accept boundary is the deadline instant or deadline+120s. 05.03.03 explicitly delegates only the *mechanism* ('single authoritative clock, submission not receipt') to /create-prd-architecture while asserting the *rule* is D-10, so the 120-second grace cannot be read as a mechanism detail — it changes which party wins in a reachable 2-minute band.
findings.failureScenario: A buyer submits a revision request 60 seconds after the auto-accept deadline on a work-for-hire mix engagement. Implementing 05.03.03 D-10: the timestamp does not precede expiry, auto-accept has fired, escrow releases, the copyright assignment executes into domain 09 and the credit emits — the request is downgraded to a recall under 05.03.03 D-05, and the buyer's revision allowance is not consumed. Implementing 05.04.01 D-04: the request lands inside the grace, auto-accept is cancelled, no rights transfer occurs, escrow stays held and a revision round opens. The two builds differ on whether a copyright assignment executed — an irreversible outcome 05.04.01 D-04 itself calls out ('a wrong auto-accept transfers copyright irreversibly').

findings.claim: 05.03.05's hostile-seller edge case and D-12 are built on a state 05.03.01 D-11 makes unreachable. D-11 hard-bounds rejection rounds at 3 and routes the third to `Requirements Deadlock` (no fault, full escrow return, no kill fee) — so a 4th rejection cannot exist, and an engagement at 3 rejections has already left the abandonment path that D-12 governs. D-12's trigger word 'Repeated' is left undefined, and the two rules also disagree on routing.
findings.evidence: 05.03-engagement-lifecycle/05.03.05-cancellation-abandonment-kill-fee.md:180 — "| Seller has rejected requirements 4 times, then claims an abandonment fee | **The attack** (DT-07) … Repeated `Requirements Rejected` (05.03.01 D-03) **caps the fee at 0% and routes the auto-close to 24 instead** (D-12). |"  ·  CONTRADICTED BY 05.03-engagement-lifecycle/05.03.01-order-lifecycle-requirements-gating.md:231 — "| D-11 | **Rejection rounds are bounded at 3. The third opens `Requirements Deadlock`: no fault, full escrow return, no kill fee, mutual release offered; 24 only if contested** |"
findings.forcedInvention: The implementer must invent the integer threshold at which 'Repeated Requirements Rejected' fires D-12. The only reachable value below D-11's hard bound is 2, which neither file states; and they must choose between D-11's routing (Deadlock → mutual release, 24 only if contested) and D-12's routing (auto-close routed to 24 for review unconditionally).
findings.failureScenario: A seller rejects the buyer's stems twice, then goes silent while the buyer does not re-supply. At day 45 the abandonment auto-close fires. Under D-12 with threshold 2, the fee caps at 0% and the close is routed to domain 24 for human review. Under D-12 with threshold 3+, the rule never triggers and the seller collects the pre-gate >14d 25% fee — the exact fault-laundering payout DT-07 exists to prevent. Separately, a third rejection produces `Requirements Deadlock` under D-11 (buyer must be offered mutual release, 24 only on contest) but an unconditional 24 referral under D-12; the two builds route a real case to different teams.

findings.claim: No file states what happens to the abandonment clock when the seller exercises `Requirements Rejected` after the gate has passed. 05.03.01 D-12 fixes the clock to 'gate open' with no reset rule for re-opening; 05.03.05 D-10 says only the awaited act resets it; the `Requirements Rejected` state row says 'clock stopped' without naming which of the two clocks. Both readings produce a defect the domain's own fault model forbids.
findings.evidence: 05.03-engagement-lifecycle/05.03.01-order-lifecycle-requirements-gating.md:232 — "| D-12 | **The abandonment clock at the gate runs from gate open, not from last buyer activity** … The gate reports elapsed-since-open; 05.03.05 owns the threshold. |"  ·  05.03.01:149 — "| Requirements Rejected | Seller sends material back (D-03) | Reason bound to the failing items; `round N of 3`; clock stopped. |"  ·  05.03.05-cancellation-abandonment-kill-fee.md:278 — "| D-10 | The abandonment clock is reset **only by the act being waited on** — never by activity."  ·  The two carve-outs that DO suspend buyer fault are enumerated and neither is rejection: 05.03.01 D-04 — "Two carve-outs: D-10 and D-11" (upstream dependency; deadlock).
findings.forcedInvention: The implementer must invent whether a seller-initiated rejection (a) restarts the abandonment clock from the new gate-open, (b) leaves it accruing from the original gate-open, or (c) stops it indefinitely as the state row's bare 'clock stopped' suggests.
findings.failureScenario: Buyer supplies a complete stem set on day 40 of the 45-day buyer-side abandonment clock; the gate passes; on day 41 the seller rejects it under D-03. Reading (b): the clock keeps accruing and the engagement auto-closes on day 45 at the pre-gate >14d rate of 25% against the buyer — penalising a buyer who supplied everything asked and was rejected, which D-04's fault model exists to prevent. Reading (c): no abandonment clock runs at all after any rejection, so a single rejection makes the engagement eternal, defeating 05.03.05 D-04's requirement that 'Silence must terminate' and leaking the seller's capacity slot forever.

This is a documented oversight, not a convention: the sibling 05.05 and 05.07 CX files were both correctly updated for exactly this pattern, and 05.03.05 flags the pickup as outstanding.

Needs pickup in Step 6. |"  ·  05.03-engagement-lifecycle-cx.md:82 — "5. **State transition conflict**: A revision request arriving at the instant auto-accept fires … precedence rule `[PENDING]`." — but 05.03.03:222 states D-10 and 05.04.01:213 states D-04.  ·  CONTRAST with the correctly-updated siblings: 05.05-multi-party-supply-cx.md CX-01 Q5 — "the buyer-recorded approval timestamp is the commit instant (`05.05.01` D-05)"; 05.07-custodial-physical-services-cx.md:41 — "`[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]`, tracked as **05.07 Q-04**".
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer working the sub-domain CX layer reads both races as undecided and must either invent a precedence rule or stall, when D-16 and D-10/D-04 already exist two files away. Neither marker carries an owner or a deferral stage, so neither is discoverable as tracked work.
findings.failureScenario: An implementer builds the milestone settlement path from the 05.03 CX file's synthesis questions, sees the delivery-vs-cancellation race marked `[PENDING]` with no owner, and implements last-write-wins by timestamp. A seller delivers stage 4 seconds before the buyer's cancellation lands; the cancellation wins the timestamp race and stage 4 is swept into the cancellation settlement, contradicting D-16 ('Delivery wins') and depriving the seller of a delivered stage worth 100% of that tranche.

findings.claim: 05.03.02's edge-case table marks 'Rights transfer at which milestone?' as pending and calls it 'The feature's hardest question', while D-01 and D-06 in the same file decide it unambiguously: milestone acceptance never transfers rights; rights execute once at final acceptance.
findings.evidence: 05.03-engagement-lifecycle/05.03.02-milestones-staged-deliverables.md:46 — "| Rights transfer at which milestone? | The buyer paid for tracking but the master is not finished. Do they own the tracked stems? | `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` — see DT-01. **The feature's hardest question.** |"  ·  CONTRADICTED BY the same file's Decisions table — "| D-01 | Milestone acceptance releases the tranche; it does not transfer rights | See DT-01. Rights execute once, at final acceptance. |" and "| D-06 | Milestone acceptance is a **two-leg commit**: it releases the tranche **and** emits a credit for the accepted stage. The **rights leg is deliberately absent** — rights transfer executes once, at final acceptance (D-01). |"  ·  Corroborated externally by 05.06.03-rights-transfer-split-execution.md 'The commit has three shapes' table: "**Milestone acceptance** (05.03.02) | Tranche release | **Does not execute** — a contingent interest vests".
findings.forcedInvention: None strictly — the answer exists in the same file — but the marker asserts an open question over a ratified decision, and an implementer reading the edge-case table first must decide which of the two contradictory statements in one file governs.
findings.failureScenario: An implementer building the milestone acceptance handler reads the edge-case table, treats per-milestone rights vesting as an undecided product question, and escalates or stubs it. If they resolve it the intuitive way (buyer paid for tracking, so tracking stems transfer), milestone 1 acceptance writes an assignment into domain 09 — producing exactly the outcome DT-01 rejects, where a cancelled album leaves the buyer owning raw multitracks they cannot use and the producer having lost control of unfinished work.

findings.evidence: 05.04-delivery-qc-acceptance/05.04.01-delivery-acceptance-auto-accept.md:56 — "| **Business days** | The seller's jurisdiction's, per 05.01.06 Q-02, which owns this question. This feature inherits whatever that resolves to and must not answer it independently |"  ·  The cited owner is unresolved: 05.01-service-listings-pricing/05.01.06-turnaround-rush-service-levels.md Open Questions — "| Q-02 | Are \"working days\" the seller's jurisdiction's or the buyer's? They differ, and the answer determines who absorbs a bank holiday. | User | Step 5 deepening |"  ·  The setting is load-bearing: the same table sets "**Platform floor** | **3 business days**" and the per-craft defaults are all denominated in business days ("Mastering | 5 business days", "Album mix / full production (final acceptance) | 14 business days").
findings.forcedInvention: The implementer must decide whether to hard-code the seller's jurisdiction's calendar (as the cell's first clause states) or to treat the calendar as an unresolved input (as the cell's second clause and 05.01.06 Q-02 require).
findings.failureScenario: A UK seller delivers to a US buyer on the Friday before the UK's late-August bank holiday, on a 5-business-day mastering window. Under the seller's calendar the deadline lands one day later than under the buyer's. Because auto-accept at that deadline executes a copyright assignment and releases escrow, the two builds transfer the master on different days — and the buyer who acts on the later date loses their revision rights entirely under the earlier one.

findings.claim: 05.04.02 D-03 mandates that each QC check be classified warn-or-fail rather than binary, but no file states the classification for any of the nine enumerated checks beyond two incidental examples, and no open question tracks it. Whether a delivery publishes at all turns on this classification.
findings.evidence: 05.04-delivery-qc-acceptance/05.04.02-deliverable-spec-automated-audio-qc.md:105 — "| D-03 | Checks are warn-or-fail, with tolerances — not binary | Hard-failing a 0.2 LUFS breach is worse than the breach. |"  ·  The nine checks are enumerated without classification in the same file's 'What QC can honestly check' table: "Container/format · Sample rate / bit depth · Loudness · True peak · Clipping / DC offset · Duration · Silence · File count & naming · Channel config".  ·  Only two data points exist, both in edge cases: "| A stem is silent | … | Warn, not fail |" and "| Loudness fails by 0.2 LUFS | Hard-failing a trivial tolerance breach is worse than the breach | Tolerance bands, and a warn-vs-fail distinction per check |".  ·  Not tracked: the file's three open questions are Q-01 (where QC executes), Q-02 (who maintains spec templates), Q-03 (buyer-side QC) — none covers the classification.  ·  CONTRAST with the sibling gate, which enumerates every threshold: 05.03.01-order-lifecycle-requirements-gating.md D-08's table gives "any file's duration differs from the set's modal duration by > 100 ms", "peak amplitude < −90 dBFS end-to-end", "≥ 3 samples at 0 dBFS", "differ by > 1 BPM".
findings.forcedInvention: The implementer must invent, per check, whether a breach blocks publication or merely warns — the decision that determines whether the buyer ever sees the delivery and whether their auto-accept clock starts (05.04 D-02: 'QC gates delivery, not acceptance').
findings.failureScenario: A master is delivered at -13.2 LUFS against a -14 LUFS spec with one true-peak sample at -0.8 dBTP against a -1 dBTP ceiling. Implementer A classifies true-peak as fatal: the delivery never publishes, the seller is bounced, and the buyer's auto-accept clock never starts. Implementer B classifies it as a warning within tolerance: the delivery publishes, the clock starts, and 7 business days later auto-accept transfers the master. Same file, same spec, opposite outcomes on both payment and copyright.

findings.claim: 05.02.03's Role Lens states the union election sits with the Producer 'and not with the buyer', while the same file's Happy Path, an edge case and an open question all have the buyer electing. In the archetypal union session the Producer IS the buyer, making the Role Lens sentence unsatisfiable on its own terms.
findings.evidence: 05.02-quotes-scope-contracting/05.02.03-union-session-contracting.md:18 — "| Producer | Config | Configures whether an engagement is a union date, which is a consequential election … The Producer is usually the party who *knows* the session's status, which is why the election sits with them and not with the buyer. |"  ·  CONTRADICTED BY the same file:33 — "2. Buyer (or Producer) elects union terms when requesting a quote, and states the session type (master, demo, jingle, film/TV — each has its own scale)"  ·  and by its edge case — "| Buyer elects union terms to look legitimate but is not a signatory | The platform floored the price and templated a document for a deal it cannot back |"  ·  and by its Open Questions — "| Q-03 | What does the platform do when a buyer elects union terms but is not a signatory? Refuse, warn, or record and step back? | User | `/create-prd-security` |"  ·  The archetypal case makes the exclusion incoherent: the same file's Musician cell casts the session player as the seller ("A union session player elects union terms on their listing"), leaving the Producer as the buyer.
findings.forcedInvention: The implementer must decide whether to render the union-election control to a buyer who is not the Producer persona, and whether a buyer-initiated election is even a valid state — three statements say yes, one says no.
findings.failureScenario: A label (buyer, not a Producer-persona account) requests a quote for an AFM master session and needs union terms elected so scale floors apply. Under the Role Lens the control is not rendered to them and the quote issues below scale — the exact violation D-01's rate floor exists to prevent, harming the player. Under the Happy Path the control renders and the quote is floored correctly, but the platform has now templated a union instrument for a buyer whose signatory status is unverified (Q-03's unresolved case).

findings.claim: 05.01.02's normative axis table admits `hybrid` as a service-mode value with no launch-scope qualifier, while the axis's declared owner (05.01.05) states that a hybrid engagement is not offered as a unified engagement at launch and defers the model to /create-prd. A seller can therefore declare a mode the platform states it cannot transact.
findings.evidence: 05.01-service-listings-pricing/05.01.02-service-category-taxonomy-attributes.md:41 — "| Service mode | remote · on-location · hybrid | `05.01.05` | 1..2 | Always |"  ·  CONTRADICTED BY the declared owner, 05.01.05-remote-vs-on-location-service-mode.md:52 — "| Hybrid engagement (tracking on-location, mixing remote) | Interim: handled as two separate orders, not one unified engagement | \"Book the tracking date and the mix separately for now.\" The unified hybrid model (single engagement with staged milestones vs two linked engagements) is an architecture decision deferred to `/create-prd` (Q-01). |"  ·  and by its States table — "| Hybrid | Order mixes on-location + remote stages | Interim (launch): not offered as one unified engagement. A buyer wanting track-on-location + mix-remote places two separate orders"  ·  The cardinality already covers the multi-mode seller without a third value: 05.01.05 describes "a session player commonly sells both (\"remote, £150/song\" and \"in your room, £450/day + travel\")", which the `1..2` cardinality expresses as two values.
findings.forcedInvention: The implementer must decide whether the service-mode enum has two members or three at launch, and — if `hybrid` is selectable — what a listing declaring it does at order time, given 05.01.05 says the unified engagement does not exist.
findings.failureScenario: A producer publishes a listing with service mode `hybrid` (permitted by the 05.01.02 vocabulary). A buyer clicks Order. There is no unified hybrid engagement to create (05.01.05 Q-01 is deferred to /create-prd), no defined scheduling model (the mode fork decides queue-depth vs calendar per 05.01.05 DT-03), and no defined delivery basis (attendance vs file per 05.04.01 D-09). The order either fails at checkout or silently creates a remote engagement whose on-location leg has no room, no travel terms and no calendar hold.

findings.claim: 05.05.04 carries two bare `[PENDING]` markers — no owner, no deferral target — covering mid-chain cancellation settlement and the terminal `Broken` state. Neither is picked up by any of the file's three open questions, so two substantive behaviours are untracked rather than deferred.
findings.evidence: 05.05-multi-party-supply/05.05.04-multi-seller-bundles-curated-packages.md:55 — "| Cancellation mid-chain | Per-stage settlement across four parties, plus the partial-work problem (05.03.05 DT-03) ×4 | `[PENDING]` |"  ·  05.05.04:67 — "| Broken | A seller exits mid-chain | `[PENDING]` |"  ·  Neither is covered by the file's Open Questions, which are Q-01 ("Who is the buyer's counterparty — the assembler or the platform?"), Q-02 ("When stage 3 is late because stage 2 was late, whose SLA breached?") and Q-03 ("Does the assembler take a margin, and is it disclosed?").  ·  CONTRAST with the same file's correctly-tracked marker at :57 — "| Seller opts out after the bundle is listed | Bundle is unsellable until refilled | `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` |", which names a deferral stage.
findings.forcedInvention: The `Broken` state has a trigger and no defined behaviour, and mid-chain cancellation has no settlement rule across four sellers. The implementer must invent both, or leave a reachable terminal state undefined.
findings.failureScenario: A four-stage bundle is cancelled after stage 2 is accepted. The implementer must decide, with no rule: whether each of the four sellers' kill-fee schedules applies independently (05.03.05 D-07 defines two schedules but not their composition across a chain), who bears the downstream cascade (05.03.05 Q-06 is open and covers only the single-assembler case), and what the `Broken` state permits — refill, refund, or dispute. Four sellers' money sits in one escrow with no defined release path.

findings.claim: 05.06.02 marks the survival of a producer's points across a re-recording of the same work as `[PENDING]` with no owner and no deferral target, and none of its four open questions covers it — leaving a high-value, currently-topical commercial term untracked.
findings.evidence: 05.06-rights-warranties-transfer/05.06.02-producer-points-backend-participation.md:62 — "| Points on a recording later re-recorded | The 2020s' favourite manoeuvre | `[PENDING]` |"  ·  Not covered by the file's Open Questions: Q-01 ("Should the platform allow [points-only deals]…"), Q-02 ("Should the platform **block** a points grant it believes the buyer lacks authority to make"), Q-03 ("Where does the aggregate allocation check live if the recording does not exist yet at election time?"), Q-04 ("Does the platform show a seller an honest expected value for points").  ·  The stakes are set by the same file's D-02 — "| D-02 | Points elected here must **execute** into 09/10 at acceptance | A recorded promise is what the industry already has. Execution is the product. |" — so the participation is a live registered interest in domains 09/10, not a note.
findings.forcedInvention: The implementer must decide whether a points participation executed into 09/10 against recording A attaches to, or is extinguished by, a subsequent re-recording B of the same underlying composition — and nothing in 05.06.01's posture parameters, D-14's deferred-effect trigger vocabulary, or 05.06.03's execution paths says which.
findings.failureScenario: A producer holds 3 points on a master, executed into domain 09 at acceptance. The artist re-records the track and releases the new master. Implementer A scopes the participation to the specific sound recording: the producer's interest is silently worth zero and the platform's registered record shows a live participation that will never pay, which is the 'recorded promise' D-02 exists to eliminate. Implementer B scopes it to the composition: the producer collects on a master they had no part in, over-allocating the new recording against 09's aggregate and tripping D-04's validation for every other participant.

findings.claim: 05.07.02's state machine defines a `Disputed` state with a trigger and a bare `[PENDING]` behaviour — no owner, no deferral target — and none of the file's four open questions covers what contesting an inspection report does.
findings.evidence: 05.07-custodial-physical-services/05.07.02-third-party-inspection-verification.md:67 — "| Disputed | Report contested | `[PENDING]` |"  ·  Not covered by the file's Open Questions: Q-01 (should a gear seller's refusal be visible on their listing), Q-02 (should an inspector be barred from quoting the repair they recommended), Q-03 (does a report attach to the instrument or the transaction), Q-04 ("Who bears an inspector's error that cost a buyer £6,000" — liability, not process).  ·  The state is consequential because the report gates money in another domain: the same file's D-04 — "The inspection is a self-contained micro-engagement in domain 05; the trigger and consequence are domain 13's" — and D-02 — "The inspector is paid on **report delivery**, regardless of the report's contents or the gear deal's outcome".  ·  CONTRAST with the sibling races in the same sub-domain, which ARE tracked: 05.07-custodial-physical-services-cx.md:41 — "`[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]`, tracked as **05.07 Q-04**, mirrored at 05.07.01 Q-05 … and 05.07.03 Q-05".
findings.forcedInvention: The implementer must invent what a contested report does: whether the inspector's own escrow is frozen (contradicting D-02's pay-on-delivery rule), whether the gear escrow in domain 13 that the report gates is held, who adjudicates, and whether a disputed report may still be acted on by the gear buyer.
findings.failureScenario: A gear seller contests an inspection report that found a cracked neck heel. Implementer A freezes the inspection engagement's escrow pending domain 24 — breaking D-02, which pays the inspector for looking regardless of findings, and reintroducing the outcome-linked incentive DT-03 exists to remove. Implementer B leaves the report actionable and the gear escrow in domain 13 releases against a contested report. Neither behaviour is stated, and the state is reachable from the ordinary path.
